title: Finding an Unknown Specific Heat Capacity by Comparing Cooling Rates
notes: An unknown specific heat can be found by timing how long the liquid takes to cool through a chosen interval, then repeating the run with water in the same calorimeter.

Newton's law says the time is proportional to the heat capacity when the surface factor and the temperature limits are unchanged. So (m_u c_u + W) / t_u = (m_w c_w + W) / t_w if the water equivalent W of the cup is included.
If the question says the calorimeter has negligible heat capacity, this collapses to m_u c_u / t_u = m_w c_w / t_w.
Water is the known standard, with c_w about 4200 J kg^-1 K^-1. The unknown c is then c_u = c_w (m_w / m_u) (t_u / t_w).
The interval must be the same pair of temperatures, for example 80°C down to 70°C, and the room must not have changed between the runs.
Stir gently so the temperature is uniform, but do not add a fan. Forced air would change K between the two runs or during a run.
examples: An unknown specific heat can be found by timing how long the liquid takes to cool through a chosen interval, then repeating the run with water in the same calorimeter.
